I did you a favor by distilling the important points while still leaving links to more information. If you would expect a reply from me, you would be wise to do the same. Fortunately, I was able to quickly pull the below from the author's comments:

1) CO2 absorbs energy at wavelengths missed by water vapor 2) CO2 has a longer atmospheric residence time than does water vapor 3) Atmospheric water vapor levels are more responsive to temperature changes than are atmospheric CO2 levels; that is: CO2 is a non-condensing greenhouse gas, while water vapor is a condensing greenhouse gas 4) There's a robust, long-term correlation between CO2 and temperature 5) At best, water vapor serves as fast feedback that amplifies the warming from factors such as CO2.

My replies:

  • 1) This point doesn't even support his conclusion, as H2O also absorbs at spectra that CO2 misses. This is, of course, because the absorption and emission spectra are merely different. Unfortunately for him, the absorption spectra for CO2 has over 2x the area under the curve for IR wavelengths as water vapor does.

A more rigorous interrogation reveals the point he was trying to make works against him. The strict (read: original) definition of 'greenhouse gas' requires both absorption and emission to lie in the IR band (termed 'reemission'). What matters is the area under the emission curves in the IR band for the gases in question, and the area under the emission curve for water vapor is many multiples that of CO2.

  • 2) This is of no significance unless we also know rates of emission or removal ('sequestration'), which we don't. The important variable to track is percentage composition by gas species, and any pro-CO2 warming argument should begin with species percentages. The only purpose for knowing residence time would be to reconstruct the total mass of the species, which we can already measure with much higher precision.

  • 3) This is an observation.

  • 4) This is patently false. This isn't an 'argument' per se, which would be constructed by reasoning with a data set. This would be an observation, except it directly contradicts data. One of the links in my top level post is well cited with more information.

  • 5) This is speculation. Maybe by 'at best' he means 'best for his argument', which would imply that 'at worst' water vapor is the sole and complete cause of global warming. Of course, this would also be speculation.
